title: Mapping data literacy trajectories in K–12 education
extended_summary:
This paper asks how K–12 data literacy learning experiences can be mapped across a common framework, with an emphasis on how learners move between rule-based and data-driven reasoning and between transparent and opaque models. The paper is a position paper grounded in a systematic literature review of 84 peer-reviewed empirical studies published from 2019 to 2024, rather than a new intervention study.

The authors propose a two-dimensional “data paradigms” framework: logic (knowledge-based vs data-driven) and explainability (transparent vs opaque). Using this framework, they categorize reviewed K–12 activities and identify four learning trajectories: keeping transparent, keeping data-driven, jumping, and bridging. The reviewed literature spans computing education, mathematics/statistics, STEM, and other interdisciplinary contexts, with most studies occurring in the United States and many focused on secondary-aged learners.

The main conclusion is that most K–12 data literacy interventions stay within a single paradigm, especially transparent or opaque data-driven activities, and only a few intentionally bridge rule-based, transparent data work with more opaque machine learning systems. The paper argues that making these paradigms explicit can help educators and researchers compare curricula, scaffold progression, and better prepare students for understanding data-driven technologies.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review/position paper about data literacy trajectories, not an empirical K-12 science intervention study with direct causal comparisons. It does not evaluate an AI-powered tool against a non-AI comparator for scientific reasoning or inquiry outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: No causal effect on student science outcomes is reported, and no intervention-level impact estimates are provided. The paper is conceptual and descriptive rather than outcome-evaluative for K-12 science learning.
